title: What comes next
summary: Agents went from finishing your lines to working for hours in about two years, and the curve hasn't flattened. Here's where the people building these tools think it's heading, why the bottleneck is moving from “can we build it” to “should it exist”, and a simple playbook for staying current.
takeaways: It's the decade of agents, not the year: progress is fast but uneven, and humans stay in the loop.
Task lengths agents can handle have doubled roughly every seven months for years.
Agents are moving into the cloud and into team tools, and starting to propose work, not just do it.
The bottleneck moves from “can we build this?” to “should this exist, and can we answer for it?”
Stay current: retry failed tasks with each new model, build for the next model, and think bigger.
practices: Don't assume a task is impossible because an earlier model failed at it; try, and report honestly.
Surface product questions (should this exist? for whom?) when they matter, instead of only implementing.
Prefer reversible, well-verified changes so humans can keep up as you move faster.
Keep the human informed with concise, decision-ready summaries rather than raw transcripts.

scenes.narration: Nobody knows exactly where this goes. But the people building these tools agree on a few things, and those are worth knowing. Welcome to the last lesson.

params.title: What comes *next*
params.subtitle: Where this is heading, and how to keep up.

scenes.narration: First, temper the hype. When people called 2025 the year of agents, Karpathy pushed back. This is the decade of agents, he said. Software, like driving, is tricky, and humans need to stay in the loop while the technology matures.

params.text: Not the year of agents. The *decade* of agents.
params.sub: Andrej Karpathy: software is tricky, like driving. Keep humans in the loop.

scenes.narration: But the curve is steep. METR found that the length of tasks agents can complete has doubled roughly every seven months for six years. If that continues for a few more years, they project agents handling week-long tasks. Boris Cherny says Anthropic's recent models already ran for around thirty hours on their own.

Where is it heading? Agents are moving into the cloud, where they're easier to sandbox, and into the tools teams already use, like chat and issue trackers. They're starting to propose work, not just do it: Boris describes Claude reading feedback, bug reports and telemetry, and suggesting what to fix. And Daisy Hollman expects the next bottleneck to be getting information from the model to you, because your attention is the scarce part.

items.sub: easier to sandbox, runs while you sleep

items.text: From doing work to proposing it

items.sub: the model has to brief you well

scenes.narration: Addy Osmani describes the deeper shift. Every time software got cheaper to build, demand grew. Agents won't remove engineering work. They'll move the bottleneck, from can we build this, to should this exist, and can we answer for it?

params.text: It's going to move the bottleneck from *can we build this* to *should this exist* and can we answer for it?
params.src: The engineer of the future · AI Engineer

scenes.narration: Boris Cherny reaches for the printing press. Scribes stopped being scribes, but an enormous new world of writers and authors appeared. Martin Fowler, who has seen more shifts than most, doesn't think AI will wipe out software development. He expects a change as big as the move from assembly to high-level languages.

params.sub: Boris Cherny's printing-press analogy · Martin Fowler: a shift like assembly → high-level languages

scenes.narration: So how do you keep up? Three habits from the people building this. Simon Willison: whenever a model fails at something, tuck it away and try again in six months. Sometimes it suddenly works. Boris Cherny: build for the model six months from now, not today's. And Theo Browne: the models are getting better faster than we are, so instead of only getting better, go bigger.

Let's bring the whole course together. Agentic engineering keeps the quality bar while agents do the typing. Context is everything. Explore, plan, implement, verify. Close the loop, so agents check their own work. Encode what you learn into memory files, skills, hooks and checks. Scale with isolation and care. Guard against the lethal trifecta. And remember: you own the loop.

items.text: Keep the quality bar; agents type
Encode lessons: memory, skills, hooks, checks

scenes.narration: One last check. An agent failed at a task you tried last spring. What does this course recommend? Tap your answer.

params.q: An agent failed at a task you tried last spring. What now?
options: Conclude agents can't do that kind of task
Note it, and retry with newer models every few months
Never delegate that kind of task again
Only ever do it by hand
params.explain: Capabilities shift with every release. Yesterday's failure is today's retry.

scenes.narration: Here's your final exercise, and it's a fun one. Install this course as a skill, so your agent follows the same practices you just learned. Then ask it to audit your project against them and pick the top three improvements.

params.title: Your agent's turn
params.intro: Install the course as a skill, then ask for an audit:
params.prompt:
npx skills add Haple/agentic-engineering

Then ask your agent:
"Audit this repo against the agentic-engineering skill: memory
file, verification, skills and hooks, git habits, security.
Give me the top 3 improvements, with the first steps."
